claim: c-Type cytochromes (cyt c) are proteins that undergo post-translational modification to covalently bind heme.
source: c-Type cytochromes (cyt c) are proteins that undergo post-translational modification to covalently bind heme, which allows them to facilitate redox reactions in electron transport chains across all domains of life.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about c-type cytochromes presented in the abstract.

claim: c-Type cytochromes facilitate redox reactions in electron transport chains across all domains of life.
source: c-Type cytochromes (cyt c) are proteins that undergo post-translational modification to covalently bind heme, which allows them to facilitate redox reactions in electron transport chains across all domains of life.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about cytochrome function.

claim: Genomic evidence suggests that cyt c are involved in electron transfer processes among the Archaea, especially in members that produce or consume methane.
source: Genomic evidence suggests that cyt c are involved in electron transfer processes among the Archaea, especially in members that produce or consume the potent greenhouse gas methane.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic surveys cited in the introduction.

claim: Neither the maturation machinery for cyt c in Archaea nor their role in methane metabolism has ever been functionally characterized.
source: However, neither the maturation machinery for cyt c in Archaea nor their role in methane metabolism has ever been functionally characterized.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the study and is supported by the lack of prior functional characterization studies.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing tools were used to map a distinct pathway for cyt c biogenesis in Methanosarcina acetivorans.
source: Here, we have used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing tools to map a distinct pathway for cyt c biogenesis in the model methanogenic archaeon Methanosarcina acetivorans, and have also identified substrate-specific functional roles for cyt c during methanogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and results described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Substrate-specific functional roles for cyt c during methanogenesis have been identified.
source: Here, we have used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing tools to map a distinct pathway for cyt c biogenesis in the model methanogenic archaeon Methanosarcina acetivorans, and have also identified substrate-specific functional roles for cyt c during methanogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the growth assays on different substrates shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cyt c maturation machinery from M. acetivorans is universally conserved in the Archaea.
source: Although the cyt c maturation machinery from M. acetivorans is universally conserved in the Archaea, our evolutionary analyses indicate that different clades of Archaea acquired this machinery through multiple independent horizontal gene transfer events from different groups of Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: Different clades of Archaea acquired the cyt c maturation machinery through multiple independent horizontal gene transfer events from different groups of Bacteria.
source: Although the cyt c maturation machinery from M. acetivorans is universally conserved in the Archaea, our evolutionary analyses indicate that different clades of Archaea acquired this machinery through multiple independent horizontal gene transfer events from different groups of Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic trees showing archaeal sequences nested within bacterial clades (Figure 8).

claim: Methanogenesis contributes substantially to global methane emissions.
source: Overall, we demonstrate the convergent evolution of a novel Archaea-specific cyt c maturation machinery and its physiological role during methanogenesis, a process which contributes substantially to global methane emissions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of methanogenesis in the global carbon cycle.

claim: C-type cytochromes are found across the tree of life.
source: C-type cytochromes (cyt(s) c) are found across the tree of life, and are critical to electron transfer processes ranging from aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion of Eukaryotes to intra/extracellular electron transport in Bacteria and Archaea (Richardson, 2000; Bertini et al., 2006; Shi et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: C-type cytochromes are critical to electron transfer processes ranging from aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion of Eukaryotes to intra/extracellular electron transport in Bacteria and Archaea.
source: C-type cytochromes (cyt(s) c) are found across the tree of life, and are critical to electron transfer processes ranging from aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion of Eukaryotes to intra/extracellular electron transport in Bacteria and Archaea (Richardson, 2000; Bertini et al., 2006; Shi et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The production of a holo-cyt c requires complex post-translational processing to covalently attach iron-protoporphyrin IX (heme b) to an unfolded apo-cyt c protein.
source: The production of a holo-cyt c, that is capable of electron transfer, requires complex post-translational processing to covalently attach iron-protoporphyrin IX (heme b) to an unfolded apo-cyt c protein (Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on cytochrome maturation.

claim: Heme attachment occurs on the extracellular face of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Heme attachment occurs on the extracellular face of the cytoplasmic membrane, and, thus also requires the translocation of the apoprotein and heme across the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cytochrome maturation.

claim: The apoprotein is translocated via the Sec pathway.
source: The apoprotein is translocated via the Sec pathway (Sambongi et al., 1996; Thöny-Meyer and Künzler, 1997; Helde et al., 1997) and a set of proteins collectively known as the cyt c maturation system are involved in energy-dependent heme transport, apoprotein handling, and covalent cofactor attachment (Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010; Kranz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Three distinct systems for cyt c maturation have been identified thus far.
source: Three distinct systems for cyt c maturation have been identified thus far, and have been studied extensively in bacterial and eukaryotic model systems (Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on cytochrome maturation systems.

claim: The biogenesis of cyt c has never been functionally characterized in an archaeon.
source: However, despite growing evidence that cyt c play a vital role in electron transport processes across members of the Archaea – particularly in microorganisms that metabolize methane and other alkanes – the biogenesis of cyt c has never been functionally characterized in an archaeon.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the current study.

claim: The vast majority of cyt c containing Archaea encode homologs of the System I cyt c maturation pathway (Ccm pathway).
source: Based on genomic surveys (Allen et al., 2006; Kletzin et al., 2015; Chadwick et al., 2021) of sequenced isolates and metagenomics assembled genomes, the vast majority of cyt c containing Archaea encode homologs of the System I cyt c maturation pathway (Ccm pathway) that is widespread in members of the Bacteria and is also present in the mitochondria of some Plants and Protozoa (Kranz et al., 2009; Giegé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic surveys.

claim: The Ccm pathway is best characterized in Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, where nine to ten proteins, encoded by ccmABCDEFGH(I) and ccdA (or dsbD), are involved in cyt c biogenesis.
source: The Ccm pathway is best characterized in Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, where nine to ten proteins, encoded by ccmABCDEFGH(I) and ccdA (or dsbD), are involved in cyt c biogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most, if not all, archaeal genomes sequenced thus far lack several ccm genes (namely ccmD, ccmH, ccmI) that have been shown to be essential for cyt c biogenesis in Bacteria.
source: Curiously, most, if not all, archaeal genomes sequenced thus far lack several ccm genes (namely ccmD, ccmH, ccmI) that have been shown to be essential for cyt c biogenesis in Bacteria like E. coli, R. capsulatus, Paracoccus denitriﬁcans, Bradyrhizobium japonicum, Shewenella oneidensis, and Desulfovibrio desulfuricans (Kranz et al., 1998; Thöny-Meyer, 1997; Goddard et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by genomic surveys and citations to bacterial studies.

claim: CcmD facilitates the release of the heme-bound holo-CcmE from the CcmABCD complex in bacteria.
source: In bacteria, CcmD facilitates the release of the heme-bound holo-CcmE from the CcmABCD complex (Richard-Fogal et al., 2008), while CcmH and CcmI are a part of the protein complex involved in covalent attachment of heme to the apo-cyt c (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CcmH and CcmI are part of the protein complex involved in covalent attachment of heme to the apo-cyt c in bacteria.
source: In bacteria, CcmD facilitates the release of the heme-bound holo-CcmE from the CcmABCD complex (Richard-Fogal et al., 2008), while CcmH and CcmI are a part of the protein complex involved in covalent attachment of heme to the apo-cyt c (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The streamlined Ccm machinery found in archaeal genomes, comprised only of CcmABCEFG and CcdA, would be insufficient for the biogenesis of cyt c based on evidence from studies with bacteria.
source: As such, based on evidence from studies with bacteria, the streamlined Ccm machinery found in archaeal genomes, comprised only of CcmABCEFG and CcdA, would be insufficient for the biogenesis of cyt c.
evidence: This is an inference based on bacterial studies cited earlier.

claim: Mature cyt c proteins have been identified in many archaeal strains, such as Haloferax volcanii, Ignicoccus hospitalis, Pyrobaculum islandicum, Ferroglobus placidus, and Methanosarcina spp.
source: However, mature cyt c proteins have been identified in many archaeal strains, such as Haloferax volcanii, Ignicoccus hospitalis, Pyrobaculum islandicum, Ferroglobus placidus, and Methanosarcina spp. (Kletzin et al., 2015; Sreeramulu, 2003; Nab et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015; Feinberg et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: M. acetivorans encodes multiple cyt c proteins.
source: In contrast, M. acetivorans encodes multiple cyt c proteins (Holmes et al., 2019), can be easily cultivated in a laboratory (Sowers et al., 1993), and has state-of-the-art genetic tools (Guss et al., 2008; Kohler and Metcalf, 2012), including inducible gene expression, tests for gene essentiality, and CRISPR-Cas9-based genome editing for complex genetic manipulation (Nayak and Metcalf, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmes et al., 2019.

claim: M. acetivorans can be easily cultivated in a laboratory.
source: In contrast, M. acetivorans encodes multiple cyt c proteins (Holmes et al., 2019), can be easily cultivated in a laboratory (Sowers et al., 1993), and has state-of-the-art genetic tools (Guss et al., 2008; Kohler and Metcalf, 2012), including inducible gene expression, tests for gene essentiality, and CRISPR-Cas9-based genome editing for complex genetic manipulation (Nayak and Metcalf, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sowers et al., 1993.

claim: M. acetivorans has state-of-the-art genetic tools including inducible gene expression, tests for gene essentiality, and CRISPR-Cas9-based genome editing.
source: In contrast, M. acetivorans encodes multiple cyt c proteins (Holmes et al., 2019), can be easily cultivated in a laboratory (Sowers et al., 1993), and has state-of-the-art genetic tools (Guss et al., 2008; Kohler and Metcalf, 2012), including inducible gene expression, tests for gene essentiality, and CRISPR-Cas9-based genome editing for complex genetic manipulation (Nayak and Metcalf, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior methods papers.

claim: M. acetivorans is a methanogen that can only grow by coupling energy conservation to the production of methane gas using acetate or methylated compounds, like methanol, as a growth substrate.
source: M. acetivorans is a methanogen that can only grow by coupling energy conservation to the production of methane gas using acetate or methylated compounds, like methanol, as a growth substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. acetivorans metabolism.

claim: At least five different cyt c proteins are encoded in the M. acetivorans genome.
source: At least five different cyt c proteins are encoded in the M. acetivorans genome and these proteins contain between one and seven heme-binding motifs (Holmes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmes et al., 2019.

claim: The cyt c proteins in M. acetivorans contain between one and seven heme-binding motifs.
source: At least five different cyt c proteins are encoded in the M. acetivorans genome and these proteins contain between one and seven heme-binding motifs (Holmes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmes et al., 2019.

claim: The ccmABCEF from M. acetivorans is sufficient to produce holo-cyt c in a heterologous host, Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro.
source: To this end, we have shown that the ccmABCEF from M. acetivorans is sufficient to produce holo-cyt c in a heterologous host, Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro, that otherwise is incapable of cyt c biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro is incapable of cyt c biogenesis.
source: To this end, we have shown that the ccmABCEF from M. acetivorans is sufficient to produce holo-cyt c in a heterologous host, Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro, that otherwise is incapable of cyt c biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing M. barkeri lacks ccm genes and does not produce cyt c.

claim: Physiological analyses reveal substrate-specific phenotypes for the cyt c biogenesis pathway and cyt(s) c during growth and methanogenesis in M. acetivorans.
source: Our physiological analyses also reveal substrate-specific phenotypes for the cyt c biogenesis pathway and cyt(s) c during growth and methanogenesis in M. acetivorans.
evidence: This is supported by growth assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cyt c biogenesis genes were likely acquired in the last common ancestor of the Methanosarcinales.
source: A closer inspection of the distribution and synteny of the cyt c biogenesis genes in methane-metabolizing archaea related to Methanosarcina (i.e. belonging to the order Methanosarcinales) suggests that the cyt c biogenesis genes were likely acquired in the last common ancestor of the Methanosarcinales and have been lost in many extant clades that also do not encode any cyt c genes.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and synteny analyses shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cyt c biogenesis genes have been lost in many extant clades of Methanosarcinales that also do not encode any cyt c genes.
source: A closer inspection of the distribution and synteny of the cyt c biogenesis genes in methane-metabolizing archaea related to Methanosarcina (i.e. belonging to the order Methanosarcinales) suggests that the cyt c biogenesis genes were likely acquired in the last common ancestor of the Methanosarcinales and have been lost in many extant clades that also do not encode any cyt c genes.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 7.

claim: The streamlined Ccm machinery is conserved across Archaea.
source: Although the streamlined Ccm machinery is conserved across Archaea, our evolutionary analyses suggest that the acquisition of cyt c biogenesis in Archaea has occurred through multiple horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events with different members of the Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 8.

claim: The acquisition of cyt c biogenesis in Archaea has occurred through multiple horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events with different members of the Bacteria.
source: Although the streamlined Ccm machinery is conserved across Archaea, our evolutionary analyses suggest that the acquisition of cyt c biogenesis in Archaea has occurred through multiple horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events with different members of the Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic trees showing archaeal sequences nested within different bacterial clades (Figure 8).

claim: Eight different genes of the Ccm machinery for cyt c maturation were identified at four different chromosomal loci in M. acetivorans.
source: We used a sequence-based approach to identify homologs of eight different genes of the Ccm machinery for cyt c maturation at four different chromosomal loci in M. acetivorans.
evidence: This is supported by the genomic analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ccmABC genes (MA1428-MA1430) are located at one chromosomal locus in M. acetivorans.
source: The ccmABC genes (MA1428-MA1430) are located at one chromosomal locus and the ccmE gene (MA4149) is in a putative operon with a geranyl farensyl diphosphate synthase at another locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ccmE gene (MA4149) is in a putative operon with a geranyl farensyl diphosphate synthase at another locus in M. acetivorans.
source: The ccmABC genes (MA1428-MA1430) are located at one chromosomal locus and the ccmE gene (MA4149) is in a putative operon with a geranyl farensyl diphosphate synthase at another locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two ccmF genes (MA3305 and MA3304 renamed ccmF1 and ccmF2, respectively) are encoded in a putative operon in M. acetivorans.
source: Two ccmF genes (MA3305 and MA3304 that have been renamed ccmF1 and ccmF2, respectively), which likely represent the C- and N-terminal segments of the bacterial ccmF locus, respectively, are encoded in a putative operon.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ccmG and ccdA are found adjacent to each other on the chromosome (MA4254 and MA4255) in M. acetivorans.
source: Finally, ccmG and ccdA are found adjacent to each other on the chromosome (MA4254 and MA4255) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Markerless in-frame deletion mutants of ccmABC, ccmE, ccmF1, ccmF2, ccmG, ccdA, as well as ∆ccmF1∆ccmF2 and ∆ccmG∆ccdA double mutants were generated using Cas9-based genome editing.
source: We used our recently developed Cas9-based genome editing technology to generate markerless in-frame deletion mutants of the ccmABC locus, ccmE, ccmF1, ccmF2, ccmG, ccdA, as well as the ∆ccmF1∆ccmF2 and ∆ccmG∆ccdA double mutants.
evidence: This is supported by the methods described and the results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing of the ΔccmABC mutant showed no off-target mutations apart from the deleted locus relative to the parent strain (WWM60).
source: We picked the ΔccmABC mutant for whole-genome sequencing to screen for off-target CRISPR-Cas9 activity. Apart from the deleted locus, we did not observe any other mutations in the ∆ccmABC mutant relative to the parent strain (WWM60) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: Off-target activity is negligible during Cas9-mediated genome editing in M. acetivorans.
source: Consistent with our previous observations, these data suggest that off-target activity is negligible during Cas9-mediated genome editing in M. acetivorans (Nayak and Metcalf, 2017; Nayak et al., 2017; Nayak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and citations to prior studies.

claim: MmcA is a heptaheme cyt c that contains an N-terminal signal peptide and is likely located in the pseudo-periplasm.
source: MmcA is a heptaheme cyt c that contains an N-terminal signal peptide and is likely located in the pseudo-periplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MmcA is a highly expressed cyt c that is widely distributed in cyt c encoding members of the Methanosarcinales.
source: MmcA is a highly expressed cyt c that is widely distributed in cyt c encoding members of the Methanosarcinales (Holmes et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2021; Borrel et al., 2019) and holo-MmcA is easy to detect as it contains seven heme-binding motifs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: TAP-tagged MmcA can be successfully detected in cell lysate using an anti-Flag antibody.
source: Using this technique, we were able to successfully detect the TAP-tagged MmcA in the cell lysate (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: TAP-tagged MmcA is capable of undergoing covalent modification to generate the corresponding holo-cyt c.
source: To assay for heme attachment (formation of holo-cyt c), we used a peroxidase-based heme stain, which detects covalently bound (c-type) heme in cyt c (Feissner et al., 2003). Using this technique, we were able to verify that the TAP-tagged MmcA is capable of undergoing covalent modification to generate the corresponding holo-cyt c (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Holo-MmcA could not be detected in the ∆ccmABC, ∆ccmE, ∆ccmF2, ∆ccmF1ccmF2 mutants.
source: We were unable to detect the tagged protein or holo-MmcA in the ∆ccmABC, ∆ccmE, ∆ccmF2, ∆ccmF1ccmF2 mutants, which suggests that these genes are essential for cyt c biogenesis in M. acetivorans (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: ccmABC, ccmE, ccmF2 are essential for cyt c biogenesis in M. acetivorans.
source: We were unable to detect the tagged protein or holo-MmcA in the ∆ccmABC, ∆ccmE, ∆ccmF2, ∆ccmF1ccmF2 mutants, which suggests that these genes are essential for cyt c biogenesis in M. acetivorans (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Apo-MmcA is immediately targeted for degradation in the absence of a functional Ccm machinery.
source: Consistent with previous studies, these results also indicate that the apo-MmcA is immediately targeted for degradation in the absence of a functional Ccm machinery (Goldman et al., 1997; Feissner et al., 2006b; Allen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the inability to detect MmcA protein in ccm mutants and citations to prior studies.

claim: A faint band corresponding to holo-MmcA was detected in the ∆ccmF1 mutant.
source: Curiously, we were able to detect faint band corresponding to holo-MmcA in the ∆ccmF1 mutant (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The gene product of ccmF1 is important but not vital for cyt c biogenesis.
source: These data suggest that the gene product of ccmF1 is important but not vital for cyt c biogenesis possibly because the catalytically important residues from CcmF in E. coli are all present in CcmF2 from M. acetivorans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the detection of holo-MmcA in the ∆ccmF1 mutant and sequence alignment data.

claim: ∆ccmG and ∆ccdA single mutants as well as the ∆ccmG∆ccdA double mutant produced roughly the same amount of holo-MmcA as the parent strain.
source: Finally, we observed that ∆ccmG and ∆ccdA single mutants as well as the ∆ccmG∆ccdA double mutant produced roughly the same amount of holo-MmcA as the parent strain (Figure 2c), which indicates that these genes are not essential for disulfide bond reduction in the apo-cyt c under highly reducing laboratory growth conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: ccmG and ccdA are not essential for disulfide bond reduction in the apo-cyt c under highly reducing laboratory growth conditions.
source: Finally, we observed that ∆ccmG and ∆ccdA single mutants as well as the ∆ccmG∆ccdA double mutant produced roughly the same amount of holo-MmcA as the parent strain (Figure 2c), which indicates that these genes are not essential for disulfide bond reduction in the apo-cyt c under highly reducing laboratory growth conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that holo-MmcA is produced in the absence of these genes.

claim: The proteins encoded by ccmABCEF1F2 in M. acetivorans constitute a functional, streamlined version of the Ccm machinery for cyt c maturation.
source: Overall, using MmcA as a diagnostic cyt c, we have shown that the proteins encoded by ccmABCEF1F2 in M. acetivorans constitute a functional, streamlined version of the Ccm machinery for cyt c maturation.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic and biochemical data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria like E. coli, heme transport and holo-CcmE formation is mediated by the CcmABCD complex.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, like E. coli, heme transport and holo-CcmE formation is mediated by the CcmABCD complex (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cytochrome maturation shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In the CcmABCD complex, CcmD plays an essential role in facilitating the release of holo-CcmE from the CcmABCE adduct.
source: In the CcmABCD complex, CcmD plays an essential role in facilitating the release of holo-CcmE from the CcmABCE adduct (Kranz et al., 2009; Richard-Fogal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M. acetivorans and all other sequenced archaeal strains lack CcmD.
source: Since M. acetivorans and all other sequenced archaeal strains lack CcmD, we investigated the role of the CcmABC complex in the formation of holo-CcmE (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by genomic surveys.

claim: Tagged-CcmE was detected in the membrane fraction of the parent strain (WWM60), ΔccmABC, and ΔccmE mutants complemented with the CcmE overexpression plasmid.
source: We introduced the C-tagged CcmE overexpression plasmid in the parent strain (WWM60) as well as the ΔccmABC and ΔccmE mutants and were able to detect tagged-CcmE in protein enriched from the membrane fraction (using an anti-Strep-affinity column) by immunoblotting with an anti-FLAG antibody in all plasmid complemented strains (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Heme-bound holo-CcmE was only observed in the enriched membrane fraction of the plasmid complemented parent strain (WWM60) and ΔccmE mutant.
source: We were only able to observe the heme-bound holo-CcmE by heme staining the enriched membrane fraction of the plasmid complemented parent strain (WWM60) and ΔccmE mutant (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Overexpression of CcmE does not rescue the ccmABC lesion in the cytochrome maturation machinery.
source: Furthermore, we were unable to detect holo-cyt c, including the MmcA protein, by heme staining the total cell lysate of the ΔccmABC strain complemented with the CcmE overexpression plasmid, which indicates that overexpression of CcmE does not rescue the ccmABC lesion in the cytochrome maturation machinery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CcmABC complex transports heme to form holo-CcmE in M. acetivorans.
source: These data support the hypothesis that the CcmABC complex transports heme to form holo-CcmE in M. acetivorans.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing holo-CcmE formation requires CcmABC.

claim: In bacteria with a Ccm machinery like E. coli, a conserved histidine residue (H130) present in the HXXXY motif of CcmE covalently binds heme.
source: In bacteria with a Ccm machinery, like E. coli, a conserved histidine residue (H130) present in the HXXXY motif of CcmE covalently binds heme (Schulz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All sequenced archaea (and a few bacteria like D. desulfuricans) have replaced the histidine in the CcmE heme-binding motif with a cysteine.
source: Notably, all sequenced archaea (and a few bacteria like D. desulfuricans) have replaced this histidine with a cysteine (Figure 4a; Allen et al., 2006; Goddard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignments shown in Figure 4a and citations.

claim: Wild-type and C120A CcmE protein were successfully detected in the Strep-enriched membrane fraction.
source: We introduced these plasmids in the ∆ccmE mutant and successfully detected the wild-type and C120A CcmE protein in the Strep-enriched membrane fraction by immunoblotting with anti-FLAG antibodies (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The C120H CcmE mutant could not be detected in the membrane or soluble fraction despite repeated attempts.
source: Despite repeated attempts, we were unable to detect the C120H CcmE mutant in the membrane or soluble fraction (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C120H substitution considerably destabilizes CcmE, leading to proteolysis of the gene product.
source: This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that the C120H substitution considerably destabilizes CcmE, leading to proteolysis of the gene product.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect the C120H mutant protein.

claim: Wild-type CcmE was observed by heme staining the Strep-enriched membrane fraction.
source: Next, we were able to observe the wild-type CcmE by heme staining the Strep-enriched membrane fraction of the corresponding strain however, no heme-stained band corresponding to CcmE was detected for the C120A mutant (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: No heme-stained band corresponding to CcmE was detected for the C120A mutant.
source: Next, we were able to observe the wild-type CcmE by heme staining the Strep-enriched membrane fraction of the corresponding strain however, no heme-stained band corresponding to CcmE was detected for the C120A mutant (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Holo-MmcA or any other holo-cyt c could not be detected in the ΔccmE strain complemented with either the C120A or C120H CcmE.
source: Furthermore, we were unable to detect holo-MmcA or any other holo-cyt c by heme staining the total cell lysate of the ΔccmE strain complemented with either the C120A or C120H CcmE (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C120 residue of the CXXXY motif is important for heme attachment as well as protein stability in the archaeal CcmE.
source: These results provide strong evidence in support of the hypothesis that the C120 residue of the CXXXY motif is important for heme attachment as well as protein stability in the archaeal CcmE.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing the C120A and C120H mutants cannot bind heme and the C120H mutant is unstable.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro has the same codon usage pattern as M. acetivorans.
source: We chose M. barkeri Fusaro as a heterologous host for this study as it has the same codon usage pattern as M. acetivorans, contains an intact pathway for heme b synthesis, and is known to produce b type cytochromes, but does not encode any of the ccm genes or cyt c in its genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. barkeri Fusaro.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro contains an intact pathway for heme b synthesis.
source: We chose M. barkeri Fusaro as a heterologous host for this study as it has the same codon usage pattern as M. acetivorans, contains an intact pathway for heme b synthesis, and is known to produce b type cytochromes, but does not encode any of the ccm genes or cyt c in its genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. barkeri Fusaro.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro is known to produce b type cytochromes.
source: We chose M. barkeri Fusaro as a heterologous host for this study as it has the same codon usage pattern as M. acetivorans, contains an intact pathway for heme b synthesis, and is known to produce b type cytochromes, but does not encode any of the ccm genes or cyt c in its genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. barkeri Fusaro.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro does not encode any of the ccm genes or cyt c in its genome.
source: We chose M. barkeri Fusaro as a heterologous host for this study as it has the same codon usage pattern as M. acetivorans, contains an intact pathway for heme b synthesis, and is known to produce b type cytochromes, but does not encode any of the ccm genes or cyt c in its genome.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: M. barkeri Fusaro does not produce cyt c.
source: To confirm that M. barkeri Fusaro does not produce cyt c, we assayed the cell lysate with the peroxidase-based heme stain for cyt c described earlier. Using this technique, we did not detect any signal of cyt c in M. barkeri Fusaro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the heme stain data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A band corresponding to the TAP-tagged MmcA was detected by immunoblotting and heme staining in M. barkeri strains expressing both mmcA and ccm genes.
source: We were able to detect a band corresponding to the TAP-tagged MmcA by immunoblotting with anti-FLAG antibodies and heme staining in M. barkeri strains expressing both mmcA and ccm genes (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot and heme stain data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The ccmABCEF1F2 genes in M. acetivorans encode a complete, functional, and streamlined version of the System I cytochrome c maturation machinery.
source: These results clearly indicate that the ccmABCEF1F2 genes in M. acetivorans encode a complete, functional, and streamlined version of the System I cytochrome c maturation machinery previously characterized in Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the heterologous expression data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Multiple cyt(s) c are encoded in the genome of M. acetivorans.
source: Multiple cyt(s) c are encoded in the genome of M. acetivorans and some of them, like MmcA, are associated with the electron transport chain; yet the cyt c maturation machinery does not seem to be essential under standard growth conditions (i.e. in medium with trimethylamine hydrochloride (TMA) as the sole carbon and energy source).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and prior studies.

claim: The cyt c maturation machinery does not seem to be essential under standard growth conditions (i.e. in medium with TMA as the sole carbon and energy source).
source: Multiple cyt(s) c are encoded in the genome of M. acetivorans and some of them, like MmcA, are associated with the electron transport chain; yet the cyt c maturation machinery does not seem to be essential under standard growth conditions (i.e. in medium with trimethylamine hydrochloride (TMA) as the sole carbon and energy source).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability to generate ccm deletion mutants.

claim: MmcA is associated with the membrane-associated Rnf complex that catalyzes the transfer of electrons between ferredoxin and methanophenazine coupled to Na+ translocation.
source: In these analyses, the ΔccmE and ΔccmABC mutants represent lesions in the Ccm pathway that would prevent maturation of all expressed cyt c, whereas the ∆mmcA mutant represents an in-frame deletion in a specific cyt c found in the membrane-associated Rnf (Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation) complex that catalyzes the transfer of electrons between ferredoxin and methanophenazine (a membrane-bound electron carrier) coupled to Na+ translocation (Wang et al., 2011; Schlegel et al., 2012; Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: During methylotrophic growth on compounds like TMA, methanol or DMS, cells disproportionate the methylated compound to produce carbon dioxide and methane in a 3:1 ratio.
source: During methylotrophic growth, on compounds like TMA, methanol or dimethyl sulfide (DMS), cells disproportionate the methylated compound to produce carbon dioxide and methane in a 3:1 ratio (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b and 1d).
evidence: This is established knowledge about methylotrophic methanogenesis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: During growth on acetate via the acetoclastic pathway, the substrate undergoes dismutation to produce carbon dioxide and methane in a 1:1 ratio.
source: In contrast, during growth on acetate, via the acetoclastic pathway, the substrate undergoes dismutation to produce carbon dioxide and methane in a 1:1 ratio (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is established knowledge about acetoclastic methanogenesis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Substantially slower growth than the parent strain was observed for the ccm-deletion mutants (∆ccmABC and ∆ccmE) as well as the cyt c deletion mutant (∆mmcA) under all conditions tested.
source: We observed substantially slower growth than the parent strain for the ccm-deletion mutants (∆ccmABC and ∆ccmE) as well as the cyt c deletion mutant (∆mmcA) under all conditions tested; however, the magnitude of the growth defect varied dramatically (Figure 6; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No growth was detected for the ccm-deletion mutants or the ΔmmcA mutant in growth medium with acetate as the sole substrate over the course of 7 weeks.
source: In growth medium with acetate as the sole substrate, we did not detect any growth for the ccm-deletion mutants or the ΔmmcA mutant (over the course of 7 weeks), which indicate that holo-MmcA and, possibly, other cyt c produced by the Ccm pathway are essential for acetoclastic methanogenesis (Figure 6c; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Holo-MmcA and, possibly, other cyt c produced by the Ccm pathway are essential for acetoclastic methanogenesis.
source: In growth medium with acetate as the sole substrate, we did not detect any growth for the ccm-deletion mutants or the ΔmmcA mutant (over the course of 7 weeks), which indicate that holo-MmcA and, possibly, other cyt c produced by the Ccm pathway are essential for acetoclastic methanogenesis (Figure 6c; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of mutants to grow on acetate.

claim: Cyt c are not essential but important during growth on methylated compounds.
source: In contrast, cyt c are not essential but important during growth on methylated compounds, however, the growth characteristics of each mutant varied substantially (Figure 6a, b and d; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data showing slower but detectable growth on methylated compounds.

claim: On TMA and DMS, the ccm-deletion mutants as well as the ∆mmcA mutant had a slower growth rate compared to the parent (WWM60) but were indistinguishable from each other.
source: On TMA and DMS, the ccm-deletion mutants as well as the ∆mmcA mutant had a slower growth rate compared to the parent (WWM60) but were indistinguishable from each other (Figure 6a and d; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 6a and d.

claim: MmcA is the sole physiologically relevant cyt c during growth on TMA and DMS.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that although MmcA is dispensable, it is the sole physiologically relevant cyt c during growth on TMA and DMS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ccm mutants and mmcA mutants have indistinguishable growth phenotypes on TMA and DMS.

claim: On methanol, the ccm-deletion mutants grew significantly slower than the parent (WWM60) compared to the ∆mmcA mutant.
source: In contrast, on methanol, the ccm-deletion mutants grew significantly slower than the parent (WWM60) compared to the ∆mmcA mutant (Figure 6b; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: MmcA is the predominant cyt c synthesized on methanol and is vital for growth, but other cyt c encoded in the genome also play a minor but physiologically relevant role.
source: These data suggest that MmcA is the predominant cyt c synthesized on methanol, and is vital for growth, but other cyt c encoded in the genome also play a minor but physiologically relevant role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ccm mutants grow slower than mmcA mutants on methanol.

claim: The role of individual cyt(s) c can vary in a substrate-specific manner.
source: Our growth analyses underscore the importance of cyt c on the physiology of M. acetivorans and highlight that the role of individual cyt(s) c can vary in a substrate-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by the differential growth phenotypes observed on different substrates.

claim: The Ccm machinery and cyt c proteins are absent in M. barkeri Fusaro.
source: Even though cyt c are important for optimal growth and methanogenesis in M. acetivorans, the Ccm machinery and cyt c proteins are absent in the close relative M. barkeri Fusaro.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data.

claim: Either all genes of the Ccm machinery are present in a Methanosarcina strain or the whole machinery is completely absent.
source: Either all genes of the Ccm machinery are present in a strain or the whole machinery is completely absent (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The strains that encode the Ccm machinery are not monophyletic.
source: The strains that encode the Ccm machinery are not monophyletic, that is, the Ccm machinery is not just present in one single clade of Methanosarcina strains.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The Ccm machinery was present in the last common ancestor of extant Methanosarcina spp. and strains like M. barkeri Fusaro have lost these genes.
source: This observation strongly supports the hypothesis that the Ccm machinery was present in the last common ancestor of extant Methanosarcina spp. and strains like M. barkeri Fusaro have lost these genes (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and synteny data.

claim: Strains like M. barkeri MS and M. vacuolata contain a truncated ORF that has sequence homology to the C-terminus of ccmE likely as a scar of a gene loss event.
source: Notably, strains like M. barkeri MS and M. vacuolata contain a truncated ORF (192 and 195 bp, respectively) that has sequence homology to the C-terminus of ccmE likely as a scar of a gene loss event (Figure 7a and b).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 7a and b.

claim: The Ccm machinery is broadly distributed in methanogens and anaerobic methanotrophic (ANME) archaea across the Methanosarcinaceae.
source: The Ccm machinery is broadly distributed in methanogens and anaerobic methanotrophic (ANME) archaea across the Methanosarcinaceae suggesting an important role for cyt c in methane metabolism across this clade (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ccm machinery is universally conserved in some genera like Methanococcoides, Methanosalsum, and Methanohalobium.
source: While the Ccm machinery is universally conserved in some genera, like Methanococcoides, Methanosalsum, and Methanohalobium, this whole machinery seems to have been lost in methanogenic isolates from members of other genera, like Methanosarcina, Methanolobus, and Methanomethylovorans (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ccm machinery seems to have been lost in methanogenic isolates from members of genera like Methanosarcina, Methanolobus, and Methanomethylovorans.
source: While the Ccm machinery is universally conserved in some genera, like Methanococcoides, Methanosalsum, and Methanohalobium, this whole machinery seems to have been lost in methanogenic isolates from members of other genera, like Methanosarcina, Methanolobus, and Methanomethylovorans (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ccm machinery and cyt c proteins in methanogens within the Methanosarcinaceae are lost frequently likely as an adaptation to certain environmental conditions.
source: Taken together, while widely distributed, the Ccm machinery and cyt c proteins in methanogens within the Methanosarcinaceae are lost frequently likely as an adaptation to certain environmental conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution patterns and is speculative about the adaptive significance.

claim: One or more clades comprising of strains belonging to the order Methanosarcinales is nested within clades derived from different bacterial groups for each of the ccm genes.
source: For each of the ccm genes, one or more clades comprising of strains belonging to the order Methanosarcinales is nested within clades derived from different bacterial groups (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic trees shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: The Ccm machinery in the Methanosarcinales was acquired by HGT from bacteria.
source: Based on these trees, it is evident that Ccm machinery in the Methanosarcinales was acquired by HGT from bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic trees showing archaeal sequences nested within bacterial clades.

claim: Different ccm genes were likely acquired from different bacteria.
source: It is also likely that different ccm genes were acquired from different bacteria, which is further corroborated by the observation that these genes are not present in an operon contrary to their chromosomal arrangement in bacterial strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic trees and genomic organization.

claim: The streamlined Ccm machinery, which lacks CcmDHI, is not ancestral to the Archaea.
source: Taken together, the streamlined Ccm machinery, which lacks CcmDHI, is not ancestral to the Archaea, rather it has been acquired through multiple inter-domain HGT events between Archaea and Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses showing HGT from bacteria.

claim: The streamlined Ccm machinery has been acquired through multiple inter-domain HGT events between Archaea and Bacteria.
source: Taken together, the streamlined Ccm machinery, which lacks CcmDHI, is not ancestral to the Archaea, rather it has been acquired through multiple inter-domain HGT events between Archaea and Bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Unique features of the archaeal cell may render CcmHDIG and CcdA dispensable such that a streamlined Ccm machinery comprising of CcmABCEF is sufficient for cyt c maturation in Archaea.
source: While it is not possible to rule out the role of historical contingency in the notable absence of CcmDHI, it is tempting to speculate that unique features of the archaeal cell render CcmHDIG and CcdA dispensable such that a streamlined Ccm machinery comprising of CcmABCEF is sufficient for cyt c maturation in Archaea.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why archaea lack certain ccm genes.

claim: Cyt c are widely found in members of the Archaea where they catalyze numerous electron transfer processes that facilitate microbial interactions and fuel biogeochemical cycles.
source: Cyt c are widely found in members of the Archaea where they catalyze numerous electron transfer processes that facilitate microbial interactions and fuel biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of cytochromes in archaea.

claim: In the vast majority of eukaryotes, a single protein called cyt c heme lyase is involved in the biogenesis of cyt c.
source: In the vast majority of eukaryotes, a single protein called cyt c heme lyase is involved in the biogenesis of cyt c (Kranz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Bacteria contain more complex pathways for cyt c biogenesis that are fine-tuned to work with lower concentrations of heme.
source: In contrast, bacteria contain more complex pathways that are fine-tuned to work with lower concentrations of heme (Kranz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The Ccm machinery requires at least nine to ten proteins (CcmABCDEFGH(I) and CcdA/DsbD) that work in concert for the biogenesis of cyt c.
source: The most complex of these pathways, called the Ccm machinery, requires at least nine to ten proteins (CcmABCDEFGH(I) and CcdA/DsbD) that work in concert for the biogenesis of cyt c.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the bacterial Ccm machinery.

claim: The biochemical details of the Ccm machinery in bacteria has been studied in great detail using model systems over the past few decades.
source: The biochemical details of the Ccm machinery in bacteria has been studied in great detail using model systems over the past few decades and the role of each ccm gene is well established at this point (Kranz et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Orthologs of at least three proteins (CcmD, CcmH, and CcmI) that are absolutely critical for cyt c maturation in bacteria are universally absent in archaeal genomes.
source: Previous research has shown that archaea encode some components of the bacterial Ccm machinery (Allen et al., 2006; Kletzin et al., 2015), however, orthologs of at least three proteins (CcmD, CcmH, and CcmI) that are absolutely critical for cyt c maturation in bacteria are universally absent in archaeal genomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genomic surveys.

claim: There are three key differences between the Ccm machinery in Bacteria and Archaea.
source: Based on our findings, there are three key differences between the Ccm machinery in Bacteria and Archaea.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental findings.

claim: ccmD is uniformly absent in archaeal genomes.
source: While ccmD seems to be uniformally absent in archaeal genomes (Allen et al., 2006), it is universally present in bacterial genomes and is essential for cyt c biogenesis in a number of strains ranging from E. coli and Rhodobacter capsultus to D. desulfuricans (Kranz et al., 2009; Goddard et al., 2010; Richard-Fogal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic surveys and bacterial studies.

claim: ccmD is universally present in bacterial genomes and is essential for cyt c biogenesis in a number of bacterial strains.
source: While ccmD seems to be uniformally absent in archaeal genomes (Allen et al., 2006), it is universally present in bacterial genomes and is essential for cyt c biogenesis in a number of strains ranging from E. coli and Rhodobacter capsultus to D. desulfuricans (Kranz et al., 2009; Goddard et al., 2010; Richard-Fogal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to bacterial studies.

claim: In bacteria, CcmD is a small (69 aa long) transmembrane protein that associates with CcmABC and facilitates the release of holo-CcmE in the periplasm after heme transport and attachment.
source: In bacteria, CcmD is a small (69 aa long) transmembrane protein that associates with CcmABC and facilitates the release of holo-CcmE in the periplasm after heme transport and attachment (Richard-Fogal et al., 2008; Feissner et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In M. acetivorans, the CcmABC complex is capable of forming holo-CcmE and releasing it into the pseudo-periplasm in a CcmD-independent manner.
source: In M. acetivorans, the CcmABC complex is capable of forming holo-CcmE and releasing it into the pseudo-periplasm in a CcmD-independent manner (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: It is unlikely that the ccmD gene has been fused to ccmA, ccmB, or ccmC based on the sequence length and alignment of the archaeal genes with their bacterial counterparts.
source: It is unlikely that the ccmD gene has been fused to ccmA, ccmB, or ccmC based on the sequence length and alignment of the archaeal genes with their bacterial counterparts (Figure 8—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence alignments.

claim: The CcmD-independent mechanism for the release of holo-CcmE from CcmABC is unlikely to be linked to the CXXXY heme-binding motif in CcmE because some bacteria that encode ccmD and require this gene product for cyt c biogenesis also contain a CXXXY heme-binding motif in CcmE.
source: It is also unlikely that the CcmD-independent mechanism for the release of holo-CcmE from CcmABC might be linked to the CXXXY heme-binding motif in CcmE because some bacteria, like D. desulfuricans, that encode ccmD and require this gene product for cyt c biogenesis also contain a CXXXY heme-binding motif in CcmE (Figure 4; Goddard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with D. desulfuricans.

claim: The archaeal cytoplasmic membrane is composed of isoprenoid lipids (phytanyl units), compared to phospholipids in bacterial cytoplasmic membranes.
source: The archaeal cytoplasmic membrane is composed of isoprenoid lipids (phytanyl units), compared to phospholipids in bacterial cytoplasmic membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about archaeal membrane composition.

claim: The lipid composition of archaeal membranes might alter how CcmABC and CcmE are anchored into the membrane and render CcmD inconsequential during the formation and release of holo-CcmE.
source: This lipid composition might alter how CcmABC and CcmE are anchored into the membrane and render CcmD inconsequential during the formation and release of holo-CcmE.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why CcmD is absent in archaea.

claim: The archaeal CcmE universally contains a CXXXY heme-binding motif whereas bacterial CcmE can either have an HXXXY motif or a CXXXY motif depending on the strain.
source: Next, the archaeal CcmE universally contains a CXXXY heme-binding motif whereas bacterial CcmE can either have an HXXXY motif or a CXXXY motif depending on the strain (Kranz et al., 2009; Goddard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and sequence alignments.

claim: In E. coli, an H130C allele of CcmE can still bind heme but cannot transfer the heme to the CcmFH complex.
source: In E. coli, an H130C allele of CcmE can still bind heme but cannot transfer the heme to the CcmFH complex (Goddard et al., 2010; Enggist and Thöny-Meyer, 2003; Stevens et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A C120H mutation in M. acetivorans seems to destabilize the protein to such an extent that it can no longer be detected.
source: In contrast, a C120H mutation in M. acetivorans seems to destabilize the protein to such an extent that it can no longer be detected (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: No heme-bound CcmE was detected for the C127H allele of CcmE derived from the bacterium D. desulfuricans.
source: Similarly, no heme-bound CcmE was detected for the C127H allele of CcmE derived from the bacterium D. desulfuricans (Goddard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Cys and His residues involved in heme-binding CcmE are not interchangeable.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the Cys and His residues involved in heme-binding CcmE are not interchangeable.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with bacterial studies.

claim: Many other as yet uncharacterized features of CcmE, possibly unique to these two groups of CcmE proteins, are likely to be equally important for the formation of holo-CcmE and the transfer of heme to the apo-cyt c via interactions between CcmE and CcmF as well as other proteins.
source: In fact, many other as yet uncharacterized features of CcmE, possibly unique to these two groups of CcmE proteins, are likely to be equally important for the formation of holo-CcmE and the transfer of heme to the apo-cyt c via interactions between CcmE and CcmF as well as other proteins.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about additional features of CcmE.

claim: The cyt c synthetase complex in bacteria contains two (CcmFH or CcmFI) or three (CcmFHI) proteins depending on the strain whereas the archaeal counterpart only contains CcmF.
source: Finally, the cyt c synthetase complex in bacteria contains two (CcmFH or CcmFI) or three (CcmFHI) proteins depending on the strain whereas the archaeal counterpart only contains CcmF.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and prior knowledge of bacterial systems.

claim: In M. acetivorans, the CcmF gene is split into two coding sequences (ccmF1 and ccmF2), each of which might be derived from different bacterial groups.
source: In M. acetivorans, the CcmF gene is split into two coding sequences (ccmF1 and ccmF2), each of which might be derived from different bacterial groups (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 8.

claim: Functionally important domains of the cyt c synthetase complex including the two histidine residues that coordinate the pseudo-periplasmic heme b as well as the highly conserved WWD domain are all present in CcmF2.
source: Functionally important domains of the cyt c synthetase complex including the two histidine residues that coordinate the pseudo-periplasmic heme b as well as the highly conserved WWD domain are all present in CcmF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CcmF1 probably plays a secondary role in cyt c biogenesis.
source: CcmF1 probably plays a secondary role in cyt c biogenesis, which might explain why a small amount of holo-cyt c can still be detected in the ∆ccmF1 mutant of M. acetivorans (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some holo-cyt c is produced in the ∆ccmF1 mutant.

claim: In bacteria and Arabidopsis, CcmH/I have been shown to interact with the apo-cyt c and deliver it to CcmF.
source: In bacteria and Arabidopsis, CcmH/I have been shown to interact with the apo-cyt c and deliver it to CcmF (Kranz et al., 2009; Setterdahl et al., 2000; Meyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is unlikely that M. acetivorans and other archaea have replaced CcmH/I with a non-orthologous protein as heterologous expression of ccmABCEF1F2 in the non-native host, M. barkeri Fusaro, seems to be sufficient for cyt c biogenesis.
source: It is unlikely that M. acetivorans and other archaea have replaced CcmH/I with a non-orthologous protein as heterologous expression of ccmABCEF1F2 in the non-native host, M. barkeri Fusaro, seems to be sufficient for cyt c biogenesis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the heterologous expression data.

claim: Cyt c like MmcA are intricately coupled to growth under a variety of conditions in the marine methanogen M. acetivorans.
source: Within the Archaea, cyt c are especially enriched in the family Methanosarcinaceae wherein these proteins have likely fostered tremendous metabolic innovation (Mand and Metcalf, 2019). Our work and other studies (Holmes et al., 2019; Ferry, 2020; Holmes et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021) show that cyt c like MmcA are intricately coupled to growth under a variety of conditions in the marine methanogen M. acetivorans (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the growth assays shown in Figure 6 and citations to prior studies.

claim: Membrane-spanning multi-heme cyt c have been shown to facilitate anaerobic methane oxidation by microbial consortia comprised of ANME archaea and sulfate reducing bacteria.
source: Furthermore, membrane-spanning multi-heme cyt c have been shown to facilitate anaerobic methane oxidation by microbial consortia comprised of ANME archaea and sulfate reducing bacteria (Wegener et al., 2015; McGlynn et al., 2015; Scheller et al., 2016; He et al., 2019) and recent studies also suggest an important role for cyt c in facilitating anaerobic alkane metabolism in several members of the Methanosarcinaceae (Borrel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies suggest an important role for cyt c in facilitating anaerobic alkane metabolism in several members of the Methanosarcinaceae.
source: Furthermore, membrane-spanning multi-heme cyt c have been shown to facilitate anaerobic methane oxidation by microbial consortia comprised of ANME archaea and sulfate reducing bacteria (Wegener et al., 2015; McGlynn et al., 2015; Scheller et al., 2016; He et al., 2019) and recent studies also suggest an important role for cyt c in facilitating anaerobic alkane metabolism in several members of the Methanosarcinaceae (Borrel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: M. acetivorans is an ideal platform to perform functional analyses of diverse cyt c across the Methanosarcinaceae.
source: Since ANME and alkane oxidizing archaea are yet to be isolated in pure culture, our ability to manipulate the biogenesis of cyt c also renders M. acetivorans as an ideal platform to perform functional analyses of diverse cyt c across the Methanosarcinaceae.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic tractability of M. acetivorans and the inability to culture ANME archaea.

claim: Many of the extant lineages that lack the Ccm machinery and cyt c are found in freshwater or anthropogenic sources (like waste digestors).
source: It is also worth noting that many of the extant lineages that lack the Ccm machinery and cyt c are found in freshwater or anthropogenic sources (like waste digestors); reciprocally, the Ccm machinery and diverse cyt c are especially conserved in lineages derived from marine environments (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and habitat information.

claim: The Ccm machinery and diverse cyt c are especially conserved in lineages derived from marine environments.
source: It is also worth noting that many of the extant lineages that lack the Ccm machinery and cyt c are found in freshwater or anthropogenic sources (like waste digestors); reciprocally, the Ccm machinery and diverse cyt c are especially conserved in lineages derived from marine environments (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and habitat information.

claim: There might be environment-specific selective pressure to retain or discard cyt c and the associated biogenesis machinery.
source: This pattern is indicative of the likelihood that there might be environment-specific selective pressure to retain or discard cyt c and the associated biogenesis machinery.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed distribution patterns.
